strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem in offline RL: the need for per-dataset hyperparameter tuning of policy-constraint scale, which is costly/infeasible in many real applications.

Proposes a reasonably novel bi-level/meta-learning (MAML-style, second-order differentiable) mechanism to adaptively scale the RL/BC trade-off coefficient during training, going beyond prior 'fixed but locally reweighted' adaptive constraint methods.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 39 datasets spanning four D4RL domains (MuJoCo, Maze2d, AntMaze, Adroit), with a single fixed hyperparameter configuration outperforming several methods that require per-dataset tuning on average.

Includes theoretical analysis (Lipschitz-based bounds, performance-difference lemma application) attempting to justify why the proposed loss terms should guarantee non-negative single-step improvement, plus a longer-horizon performance-gap bound.

Good supporting analyses: learning curves of alpha showing sensible dataset/task-adaptive behavior, runtime overhead analysis showing the method is cheap when kα is tuned, and ablations isolating the effect of the robust critic architecture and each loss component (L1, L2, L3).
Reasonably thorough reproducibility details (hyperparameter tables, hardware/software specs) in the appendix.
weaknesses: There is an unresolved gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.5's derivation requires a constant w (≈30κ²) multiplying L3 for the guarantee to hold, but the practical algorithm simply sets w=1 'for simplicity,' which the authors themselves flag in Remark 4.1 without rigorously justifying why the guarantee still approximately holds in this regime. This weakens the claimed theoretical performance guarantee as a rigorous certificate for the actual method used.

ASPC's advantage is not consistent across all domains: ReBRAC (with per-dataset tuning) beats ASPC on AntMaze and Adroit, and even wPC (fixed hyperparameters) is competitive/better than ASPC on AntMaze, which somewhat undercuts the framing that a single ASPC configuration uniformly matches or exceeds carefully tuned SOTA baselines; the paper leans on the aggregate 'Total Avg' metric to make this claim, which can mask domain-level shortfalls.

Missing comparisons to some other relevant modern offline RL baselines beyond runtime (e.g., CQL is only shown in the runtime plot, not in the main performance table); no comparison with diffusion-policy-based or transformer-based offline RL methods that are increasingly used as strong baselines.

The three-term outer loss (L1, L2, L3) has a somewhat ad hoc construction motivated by loose asymptotic Taylor-expansion arguments (assuming ΔL_BC/c²_∞ ≪ 1); it is unclear how tight/valid these approximations are in the medium-to-late training regimes actually explored, and no empirical validation of the approximation quality is provided.

Only 4 random seeds are used, which may be insufficient given the very high variance observed in several AntMaze/Adroit results (e.g., large standard deviations in Table 1), making some domain-level comparisons less statistically convincing.

The performance gains partially depend on the 'robust critic' (deeper network + LayerNorm) borrowed from prior work (ReBRAC-style architecture) rather than purely from the proposed adaptive-scaling mechanism; while the ablation attempts to disentangle this, the core algorithmic contribution's standalone marginal benefit could be presented more clearly and quantitatively.

Limited discussion of computational/implementation complexity and stability of the second-order (bilevel) optimization beyond runtime, e.g., sensitivity to the TorchOpt implementation, potential for training instability in more complex environments, or failure cases beyond the reported ablations.

The evaluation remains confined to the standard D4RL benchmark; the authors acknowledge but do not address generalizability to real-world or noisier datasets, limiting evidence for broader significance claimed in the introduction.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: 39 D4RL datasets across 4 domains, plus additional OGBench experiments, with multiple ablations (robust critic, loss components, L3 formulation variants, α initialization and learning-rate sensitivity).
Demonstrates broad applicability by integrating the ASPC idea into IQL, CQL, Diffusion-QL, and FQL, showing the bilevel constraint-scaling idea is not specific to TD3+BC.

Provides theoretical analysis (mutual-constraint proposition, single-step and long-horizon performance bounds) that at least qualitatively motivates the design of the outer loss terms L2/L3, and the paper is transparent about assumptions and proofs in the appendix.
Reports runtime overhead analysis showing the second-order updates can be made cheap via a longer α-update interval without much performance loss, addressing a natural practicality concern.
Good qualitative analysis of α dynamics (task- and dataset-quality dependent behavior) that supports the intuitive story of the method and adds interpretability.
weaknesses: The headline claim that ASPC with a single hyperparameter configuration 'outperforms' meticulously tuned SOTA (e.g., ReBRAC) is only true on some aggregated averages; per-domain/per-dataset inspection (Table 1) shows ReBRAC clearly wins on most HalfCheetah tasks and several Adroit tasks, and the 'Total Avg' metric is heavily influenced by Maze2d, whose raw score scale (up to 200+) is much larger than other domains, potentially skewing the unweighted overall comparison.

The theoretical results, while formally proven, rely on strong/idealized assumptions (global Lipschitz continuity of Q and the transition kernel, an 'idealized' update satisfying ΔQ ≥ Φ) that are unlikely to strictly hold for deep neural Q-functions; the practical L3 term is obtained via a first-order Taylor approximation and an ad-hoc rescaling (setting w=1), which weakens the rigor implied by the 'theoretical performance guarantee' framing in the abstract.

Despite the 'single hyperparameter configuration' selling point, the method still contains several sensitive hyperparameters (α initialization, α learning rate, update interval kα) whose sensitivity analysis (Figures 11-12) shows substantial performance swings across domains, suggesting some hidden per-domain tuning was likely needed to select the reported defaults.

The generalization results to other backbones (Table 3, Table 4) are mixed rather than uniformly positive — several individual datasets show performance degradation when ASPC is added (e.g., IQL on halfcheetah-medium and hopper-medium, several OGBench antmaze-giant tasks with FQL+ASPC declining by double digits), which is somewhat at odds with the paper's claim of 'consistent' improvement.

The set of 'adaptive policy constraint' baselines is limited to wPC and A2PR; other recent adaptive/auxiliary-model approaches mentioned in related work (PRDC, GORL, IEPC, OAP) are not empirically compared, leaving the competitive landscape for the core claimed contribution incompletely tested.

Ablations and dynamics analyses are largely presented as domain-averaged bar/line charts, which can mask important per-task variance and failure cases (e.g., the poor AntMaze/Adroit performance is explained post hoc via a sparse-reward argument and partially patched with an additional advantage-weighting trick in the appendix, suggesting the core method alone is not fully sufficient in this setting).
